title: System calls and mmap
summary: How a program enters the Linux kernel on x86-64, what a syscall really costs and how the vDSO avoids it, and how mmap maps files and memory lazily with page faults, sharing and copy-on-write.
outcomes: Explain how the x86-64 syscall instruction passes the number, arguments and errors between user code and the kernel
Estimate syscall overhead from a per-call cost and cut it with buffering, batching and the vDSO
Compute which page a mapped byte lands in and predict zero-fill, SIGBUS and EINVAL cases for a file mapping
Explain MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE, MAP_ANONYMOUS and copy-on-write, including when writes reach the file
Decide when mmap beats explicit I/O and when a buffer pool is the safer design

lessons.title: What happens when your program calls write

blocks.md:
Your program runs in **user mode**: the CPU refuses privileged instructions, and the kernel's memory is off limits. That is what keeps one buggy program from scribbling on the disk controller or on another process. Recall from the virtual memory course that every load and store goes through page tables the kernel owns.

So how does `printf` ever reach the terminal? It asks the kernel. A **system call** (syscall) is a controlled doorway: user code names an operation by number, passes arguments in registers, and executes one special instruction that switches the CPU to kernel mode at an entry point the kernel chose in advance. User code cannot jump anywhere else inside the kernel.

On x86-64 Linux the doorway is the `syscall` instruction. The rules come from [syscall(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscall.2.html) and the comment above the kernel's entry code:

- `rax` holds the syscall number. Numbers come from the kernel's table: `read` is 0, `write` is 1, `mmap` is 9, `munmap` is 11, `getpid` is 39, `exit` is 60.
- Up to six arguments go in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `r10`, `r8`, `r9`.
- The result comes back in `rax`.

Here is the whole thing with no C library at all: write 3 bytes to stdout, then exit.

blocks.title: A raw 3-byte write to stdout in x86-64 assembly
blocks.code:
.section .rodata
msg: .ascii "hi\n"
    .text
    .globl _start
_start:
    mov  $1, %eax          # syscall number 1 = write
    mov  $1, %edi          # arg0: fd 1 (stdout)
    lea  msg(%rip), %rsi   # arg1: buffer address
    mov  $3, %edx          # arg2: count = 3 bytes
    syscall                # enter the kernel
    # back in user mode: rax = 3 or -errno
    mov  $60, %eax         # syscall number 60 = exit
    xor  %edi, %edi        # arg0: status 0
    syscall

scenes.caption: Load the syscall number. To the kernel, 1 means write. Nothing has happened yet: this is an ordinary register move in user mode.
Arguments go in the registers the ABI names: fd in rdi, buffer pointer in rsi, length in rdx. The kernel will read them from exactly these places.
syscall saves the user return address into rcx and the flags into r11, then jumps to the kernel entry point stored in a CPU register (an MSR). The CPU is now in kernel mode.
The kernel ran its write handler and returned. rax now holds the result: 3 bytes written. rcx and r11 hold whatever the CPU put there, so they are clobbered.
Same pattern for exit: number 60 in rax, status in rdi, syscall. This call never returns.

blocks.md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

What does the kernel do between `syscall` and the return? In the current source ([entry_64.S](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S)), `entry_SYSCALL_64` swaps to the kernel's per-CPU data with `swapgs`, switches to kernel page tables and a kernel stack, and pushes every user register into a `pt_regs` structure. Then `do_syscall_64` checks the number is in range and dispatches to the handler, such as `sys_write`. On the way out it restores the registers and, when the state allows it, returns with the fast `sysretq` instruction.

blocks.title: The path of one write() call

scenes.caption: Your code calls write like any C function. The libc wrapper is ordinary user-mode code that puts the number and arguments in registers.
The syscall instruction transfers control to entry_SYSCALL_64, the single entry point for 64-bit system calls. The mode switch happens here.
Registers are saved into pt_regs, then do_syscall_64 checks the number against the table size and calls the matching handler.
The handler's return value goes into rax and the kernel returns to the instruction after syscall. Back in user mode.
If rax holds a value from -4095 to -1, the wrapper treats it as an error: it stores the positive code in errno and returns -1 to your code.

blocks.md: The kernel reports errors as small negative numbers in `rax`. The kernel defines `MAX_ERRNO` as 4095, and glibc's test is literally `(unsigned long) val > -4096UL`: any raw result from -4095 to -1 is an error. The wrapper negates it into `errno` and returns -1. So the familiar "returns -1 and sets errno" contract is a C library convention layered over the raw kernel interface.

blocks.prompt: A program calls `write` on fd 7, which it already closed. The raw `syscall` returns -9 in `rax` (`EBADF` is 9). What does the C caller of `write` see?
blocks.reveal: The return value is **-1** and `errno` is **9** (`EBADF`). The wrapper saw a raw value in the range -4095 to -1, negated it into `errno`, and replaced the return value with -1. If you call `syscall(2)` through `syscall()`, the same translation happens. Only a hand-written `syscall` instruction sees the raw -9.

blocks.question: Why does the x86-64 Linux syscall convention pass the 4th argument in r10 instead of rcx, which the normal C calling convention uses?
options: The syscall instruction overwrites rcx with the user return address
The kernel needs rcx to hold the syscall number
r10 is faster to read from kernel mode
rcx is reserved for the error code
blocks.explain: The `syscall` instruction saves the return address in rcx and rflags in r11, so anything you put in rcx is destroyed by the instruction itself. The kernel's entry comment notes that arg3 arrives in r10 and must be moved to rcx to match the C ABI before calling C handlers.

blocks.question: mmap returns a pointer. The raw syscall can also fail. How does libc tell a valid address from an error in rax?
options: A valid address is never negative, so any value with the top bit set is an error
The kernel sets the carry flag on error
Values from -4095 to -1 (the top 4095 addresses) are reserved for errors; anything else is a result
mmap returns 0 on error
blocks.explain: On x86-64 Linux there is no separate error flag (the syscall(2) table lists none). Those top 4095 values lie in the kernel half of the address space, never a user mapping, so glibc treats raw results in that range as negated error codes. A user-space mapping address is a normal positive number, but checking the top bit alone would be wrong in general.

lessons.title: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them

blocks.md:
A function call costs a few cycles. A system call costs far more, in two ways. The **direct cost** is the mode switch itself: entering the kernel, saving state, returning. The **indirect cost** is what the kernel's code and data do to your caches, TLB and branch predictors while it runs: when you come back, your working set has been partly evicted.

The FlexSC paper (Soares and Stumm, OSDI 2010) measured both on a 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7. A syscall that does nothing took 79 cycles to enter and 71 to leave: **150 cycles round trip**, about 65 ns. After a single `pwrite`, the user program's instructions per cycle stayed depressed for up to **14,000 cycles** (about 6.1 microseconds) while it refilled its caches.

blocks.title: Cache lines evicted per call or call group (FlexSC, Core i7)

scenes.caption: L1 instruction-cache lines replaced by the kernel during each call (64-byte lines). Modest: 2 to 5 KB of code.
L1 data-cache lines replaced. The d-cache on that CPU held 32 KB (512 lines), so each call evicts a large fraction of it. This is the indirect cost your code pays after returning.

blocks.md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (branch speculation control) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

The direct cost is paid **per call**, not per byte. So the main lever is to make fewer calls that each do more. Writing 1 MiB one byte at a time takes 1,048,576 `write` calls. With a 4 KiB buffer it takes 256. With a 64 KiB buffer, 16. That is why stdio buffers `printf` output, why `readv` and `writev` move several buffers in one call, and why interfaces like io_uring batch many operations per kernel entry.

blocks.title: Mode-switch time to write 1 MiB vs buffer size

scenes.caption: Simplified model: calls = 1 MiB / buffer size, each paying only the FlexSC mode-switch cost. One-byte writes spend 68.4 ms just switching modes; a 4 KiB buffer cuts that 4096 times to 16.7 microseconds.

Raise the per-call cost to 1 microsecond, a stand-in for a call that does real kernel work plus cache refill. The curve shifts up but keeps its slope: every doubling of buffer size halves the call overhead.

blocks.md:
Some calls can skip the kernel entirely. Programs ask for the time constantly, so the kernel maps a tiny shared library, the **vDSO** (virtual dynamic shared object), into every process. On x86-64 it exports `__vdso_clock_gettime`, `__vdso_gettimeofday`, `__vdso_time` and `__vdso_getcpu` ([vdso(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/vdso.7.html)). glibc calls these instead of issuing a syscall.

The trick: the kernel keeps time data in a page also mapped read-only into your process. The vDSO code reads it inside a retry loop guarded by a sequence counter (if the kernel updated the data mid-read, read again), then adds the elapsed hardware counter ticks. If the clock source cannot be read from user mode, it falls back to a real syscall.

blocks.title: clock_gettime: syscall path vs vDSO path

scenes.caption: Without the vDSO, every clock read is a full syscall: mode switch in, handler, mode switch out.
With the vDSO, glibc makes an ordinary function call into code the kernel mapped into your process. No mode switch.
The kernel updates the shared time data. The vDSO reads it and checks the sequence counter, retrying if an update raced with the read, then adds hardware counter ticks.
If the clock source cannot be read from user mode, the vDSO falls back to the real syscall. Correctness is kept; only speed is lost.

blocks.md: vdso(7) states that calls served by the vDSO do not appear in `strace` output and are invisible to seccomp filters. A trace with zero `clock_gettime` lines does not mean the program never asks for the time.

blocks.prompt: You strace a server that you know calls `clock_gettime` about a million times per second. The trace shows `epoll_wait`, `read`, `write`, but not a single `clock_gettime`. Bug in strace?
blocks.reveal: No. glibc routes `clock_gettime` to `__vdso_clock_gettime`, which runs entirely in user mode, so there is no system call for strace to intercept. You would see it only if the vDSO fell back to the kernel, for example when the clock source cannot be read from user mode. To count these calls, use a user-space tool such as a uprobe on the vDSO symbol or a profiler.

blocks.md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

blocks.question: A logger issues one `write` per 40-byte log line and handles 200,000 lines per second. Which change cuts syscall overhead the most?
options: Switch from write to pwrite
Accumulate lines in a 64 KiB buffer and write when it fills or on a short timer
Call fsync after every line so the kernel batches better
Open the log file with O_APPEND
blocks.explain: Overhead scales with the number of calls. Buffering 64 KiB packs about 1,638 lines per call, so 200,000 calls per second become about 122. pwrite and O_APPEND change semantics, not call count, and fsync adds an even more expensive call per line. Keep a flush timer so a crash or a quiet period does not hold lines forever.

lessons.title: mmap: putting a file into your address space

blocks.md:
To process a file with `read`, you copy chunks from the kernel into a buffer you own, one syscall per chunk, and you manage offsets yourself. `mmap` offers a different deal: ask the kernel once to make a range of your virtual address space *stand for* the file, then use plain pointers. Byte `i` of the file is just `p[i]`.

The call is `mmap(addr, length, prot, flags, fd, offset)`. `addr` is usually `NULL` so the kernel picks a page-aligned address. `prot` is `PROT_NONE` or a bitwise OR of `PROT_READ`, `PROT_WRITE` and `PROT_EXEC`. `flags` must include exactly one of `MAP_SHARED`, `MAP_PRIVATE` or `MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE` (a stricter `MAP_SHARED`) (next lesson). `fd` and `offset` say which file bytes back the range.

blocks.caption: Sum every byte of a file through a read-only mapping. Error checks on open and fstat omitted for brevity.

blocks.md: The surprising part is what `mmap` does *not* do. It reserves the address range and records which file backs it, but it reads nothing from disk and fills no page table entries. The work happens later, one page at a time: the first touch of each page raises a **page fault**, the kernel finds the file data (reading it from disk into the page cache if needed), installs a page table entry, and restarts the instruction. This is the demand paging you met in the virtual memory course, now backed by a file instead of swap.

blocks.caption: With 4 KiB pages, byte 5000 is in page 1 at offset 904, because 5000 = 4096 + 904. In binary that is i >> 12 and i & 4095.

scenes.caption: mmap returned. 16,384 bytes of address space (4 pages) are reserved, but nothing is resident. The file has 10,000 bytes: two full pages, 1,808 bytes in page 2, none in page 3.
Read p[0]. No page table entry exists, so the CPU faults. The kernel reads page 0 of the file into the page cache (a major fault, since it needed I/O) and maps it.
Read p[5000]: page 1, offset 904. Another fault, another page mapped. Each 4 KiB page faults once; later accesses to it run at memory speed.
Read p[11000]: page 2, offset 2808, past the file's 1,808 bytes in that page. This page faults in like the others, but its bytes past end of file are zero-filled, so the read returns 0. No error.
Read p[13000]: page 3 lies wholly beyond the end of the file. The kernel delivers SIGBUS, which kills the process unless it is handled.

blocks.md:
The rules from [mmap(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html), all visible above:

- `offset` must be a multiple of the page size (`sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`), otherwise `EINVAL`. `length` need not be; the mapping covers whole pages.
- In the last partial page, bytes past end of file read as zero, and writes there are never carried to the file.
- Touching a page entirely beyond end of file raises `SIGBUS`. Writing to a read-only mapping raises `SIGSEGV`.
- You may `close(fd)` right after `mmap`; the mapping keeps the file referenced.
- The kernel reports faults it served from memory and from disk separately, as minor and major faults in [getrusage(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrusage.2.html).
`mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.
mmap is lazy. The call sets up a promise; each page is paid for with a page fault on first touch. Errors that `read` would return as a value (file truncated, disk error) arrive as signals instead.

blocks.question: You want to map a file starting at byte 5000. Page size is 4096. What do you pass, and where is byte 5000 in the result?
options: offset 5000; byte 5000 is at p[0]
offset 0; byte 5000 is at p[904]
offset 8192; byte 5000 is at p[-3192]
offset 4096; byte 5000 is at p[904]
blocks.explain: offset must be page-aligned, so round 5000 down to 4096 and add the remainder yourself: 5000 - 4096 = 904. Passing 5000 fails with EINVAL. Remember to extend length by the same 904 bytes so the end of the range you want is still covered.

blocks.question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
blocks.explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

blocks.md: Where do the bytes behind a file mapping live? In the **page cache**: the kernel's in-memory copy of file pages, shared by everyone using that file. `read` copies bytes out of a page cache page into your buffer. A file mapping instead points your page table entry *at the page cache page itself*. No copy, and no syscall per access, which is exactly the benefit database developers were after (Crotty, Leis and Pavlo, CIDR 2022).

blocks.title: First and second touch of a mapped page

scenes.caption: A loads from a mapped address. The MMU finds no valid page table entry and raises a page fault into the kernel.
The kernel finds which file and offset back this address. The page is not in the page cache, so it must read the disk: a major fault.
The kernel installs a page table entry pointing at the page cache page and returns. The CPU retries the same load, which now succeeds.
Process B maps the same file and touches the same page. It still faults (its own page table is empty), but the data is already cached: a minor fault, no disk I/O.

blocks.md:
The flags decide what happens on a **write**:

- `MAP_SHARED`: writes go to the shared page cache page. Other processes mapping the same region see them, and the kernel eventually writes them to the file.
- `MAP_PRIVATE`: a private **copy-on-write** mapping. Reads share the page cache page, but the first write to a page makes the kernel copy it into a fresh page that only this process sees. The file never changes. The kernel's page fault code has names for these cases: `do_read_fault`, `do_shared_fault`, `do_cow_fault`.

blocks.title: One file page, a shared mapper and a private mapper

scenes.caption: Both processes read the page. Their page table entries point at the same physical page cache page. One copy of the data in RAM.
A writes through its MAP_SHARED mapping. The page cache page changes in place and is marked dirty. Any other MAP_SHARED mapper sees the new bytes immediately.
Whether B, a MAP_PRIVATE mapper that has not written this page, sees A's change is unspecified by mmap(2). Do not rely on it either way.
B writes. Its entry was read-only, so the write faults; the kernel copies the page into a new private page and repoints B there. A and the file never see B's change.
The kernel writes A's dirty page to disk at a time of its choosing, or when A calls msync. B's private copy is never written to the file.

blocks.md:
When do `MAP_SHARED` writes reach the disk? [msync(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/msync.2.html) says that without `msync` there is no guarantee they are written back before `munmap`. `MS_SYNC` requests the write and waits for it; `MS_ASYNC` schedules it and returns (on Linux it is a no-op, since the kernel already tracks dirty pages). The kernel is also free to write dirty pages back earlier on its own, which matters for databases (next lesson).

`MAP_ANONYMOUS` mappings have no file at all: pages start zero-filled. That is how allocators get large blocks. glibc `malloc` uses `mmap` for requests at or above `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD`, which starts at 128 KiB and adjusts upward dynamically as large blocks are freed ([mallopt(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mallopt.3.html)). Freeing such a block returns it to the kernel with `munmap`.

Copy-on-write is also how `fork` stays cheap: the child gets copies of the parent's page tables, both point at the same physical pages, and a page is duplicated only when one side writes it ([fork(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)). A worked example with 4 KiB pages: a parent holding 1 GiB of written anonymous memory has 262,144 pages. Right after `fork`, physical use is still 262,144 pages. If the child then writes a quarter of them, 65,536 pages are copied.

blocks.title: Physical 4 KiB pages: 1 GiB process forks

scenes.caption: Before fork: the parent owns all 262,144 pages.
Right after fork: nothing is copied. All 262,144 pages are shared, marked read-only in both page tables.
The child writes 25% of the pages (65,536). Each write faults and copies one page. Total physical pages: 196,608 + 65,536 + 65,536 = 327,680, or 1.25 GiB.

blocks.question: Two worker processes map the same data file. Worker 1 uses MAP_SHARED and writes a record. Worker 2 uses MAP_PRIVATE and has only read that page. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Worker 2 sees the new record immediately
Worker 2 never sees the new record
Whether worker 2 sees it is unspecified, so code must not depend on it
The write fails because a private mapping of the page exists
blocks.explain: mmap(2) states it is unspecified whether changes made to the file after the mmap call are visible in a MAP_PRIVATE mapping. In practice an untouched private page often still points at the page cache page, but once worker 2 writes that page it has its own copy. Use MAP_SHARED in both if they must see each other's writes.

blocks.question: A program writes 100 MB into a MAP_SHARED file mapping, then the machine loses power before the program calls msync or munmap. What can you say about the file?
options: None of the writes are in the file
All of the writes are in the file, because shared mappings write through
The file is restored from the page cache on reboot
Any subset of the dirty pages may have reached the file
blocks.explain: The kernel writes dirty pages back whenever it chooses, so some may have reached the disk and others not, in no order you control. msync with MS_SYNC is how you force a range to disk and wait. This lack of ordering is why mmap-based databases still need a write-ahead log or shadow paging (as LMDB uses) to stay consistent.

lessons.title: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it

blocks.md: mmap shines when data is read often, fits comfortably in memory, and is shared. Executables and shared libraries are mapped this way; the kernel's own documentation for `max_map_count` (default 65530 mappings per process) says mappings come from malloc, direct mmap, mprotect and madvise calls, and loading shared libraries. Read-mostly lookup tables and indexes loaded by several processes get one copy in the page cache, with no copy into each process and no syscall per access. LMDB relies on mmap entirely, and SQLite offers it as an option.

It hurts when the data is much larger than memory and the program needs control. Crotty, Leis and Pavlo ("Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?", CIDR 2022) list four problems:

1. **Transactional safety**: the OS can write a dirty page to the file at any moment, even a pinned one, so a half-finished transaction can reach disk.
2. **I/O stalls**: any pointer dereference can block on a disk read, and there is no asynchronous way to fault a page in.
3. **Error handling**: an I/O error arrives as `SIGBUS` at whatever instruction touched the page, not as a return value.
4. **Performance**: page table contention, single-threaded page eviction (`kswapd`), and TLB shootdowns, inter-processor interrupts that flush stale entries from every core's TLB when a page is unmapped.

blocks.title: Random reads: explicit I/O (fio) vs mmap, simplified

scenes.caption: From the paper's text: 100 threads doing random reads on one NVMe SSD. fio holds close to 900K reads per second throughout.
mmap with MADV_RANDOM tracks fio for the first 27 seconds, while the page cache still has free memory.
The page cache is full, so every new page needs an eviction. Throughput drops to nearly zero for about five seconds.
It recovers to roughly half of fio, limited by eviction overhead: shootdowns, one kswapd thread, page table contention. The 40 s end point is illustrative; phases are from the paper.

blocks.md: The paper's summary: mmap did well only on a single SSD during the initial loading phase; once eviction began, or with multiple SSDs, it was 2 to 20 times worse than fio. For sequential scans across 10 SSDs the gap was roughly 20 times. MongoDB (its original MMAPv1 engine), InfluxDB and SingleStore all moved off mmap-based file I/O after hitting these problems.

If you do use mmap, you can steer the kernel with hints ([madvise(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/madvise.2.html)):

- `MADV_SEQUENTIAL`: read ahead aggressively, pages may be freed soon after use. Good for scans.
- `MADV_RANDOM`: read-ahead is less useful. Good for point lookups.
- `MADV_WILLNEED`: start reading this range now.
- `MADV_DONTNEED`: done with this range; the kernel may free it, and later accesses refetch from the file (or get zeros for private anonymous memory).

`MAP_POPULATE` prefaults the whole mapping at `mmap` time instead of on first touch, and `mincore` reports which pages are resident.

blocks.title: Page faults to first-touch 1 GiB of anonymous memory

scenes.caption: With 4 KiB pages, touching 1 GiB takes 262,144 first-touch faults, each a kernel entry.

Transparent huge pages map 2 MiB per fault: 512 faults, the 512x cut the kernel docs describe. The bigger lasting win is fewer TLB misses. Simplified: THP applies to anonymous memory and tmpfs/shmem, not regular file mappings.

blocks.md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen` or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` instead of clobbering.

Use mmap for read-mostly data that fits in memory and benefits from sharing. When data far exceeds memory, or you need control over when writes reach disk and how I/O errors surface, explicit I/O with your own buffer pool wins.

blocks.question: You are building a key-value store for datasets 10 times larger than RAM on fast NVMe drives, with transactional writes. Which design does the CIDR 2022 evidence favor?
options: mmap the whole file with MAP_SHARED and rely on msync at commit
A user-space buffer pool with explicit reads and writes (for example pread or io_uring)
mmap with MADV_RANDOM, since it matched fio in the paper
mmap with MAP_POPULATE so all pages are resident up front
blocks.explain: MADV_RANDOM matched fio only until the page cache filled; then eviction overhead cut throughput to about half. MAP_SHARED also lets the OS write uncommitted pages at any time. MAP_POPULATE cannot make 10x RAM resident. A buffer pool controls eviction, write ordering and error handling.

blocks.question: Eight worker processes each need read-only access to the same 2 GiB lookup table on a machine with 64 GiB of RAM. Which approach uses the least memory?
options: Each worker mmaps the file with PROT_READ
Each worker reads the file into its own malloc buffer
Each worker mmaps with MAP_ANONYMOUS and copies the file in
One worker reads it and sends it to the others over a pipe
blocks.explain: Read-only file mappings in all eight workers point at the same page cache pages, so the table occupies about 2 GiB once. Reading into private buffers keeps eight copies (16 GiB) plus the page cache copy. Anonymous memory is private per process too. This read-mostly, fits-in-RAM, shared case is where mmap clearly wins.
